title: monday.com vs Gigxomi for Video Editing Workflows
excerpt: Compare monday.com work management with Gigxomi's dedicated workflow for video editing clients, managers, editors, reviews, and payouts.
seoDescription: monday.com vs Gigxomi for video editing agencies: compare work management with client, manager, editor, review, delivery, and payout workflows.
featuredImageAlt: monday.com versus Gigxomi video editing workflow guide
introduction: monday.com work management gives teams colorful boards, configurable columns, views, dashboards, templates, forms, and automations for many types of work. Gigxomi is designed specifically for video editing businesses. The decision is between a visual toolkit your operations team configures and a specialist workflow that already understands agency roles and commercial delivery.
verdict: Choose monday.com when visual board management, cross-team reporting, templates, and customizable automations are the priority. Choose Gigxomi when your agency wants to connect messaging-led client intake with editors, managers, review, delivery, accounting, and payouts. monday.com is broader and more configurable; Gigxomi is more opinionated about the editing-business lifecycle.

sections.heading: Why agencies like monday.com's visual boards
paragraphs: A production manager can scan a well-designed monday.com board and understand status quickly. Columns for client, format, editor, deadline, priority, review round, and publish channel create a familiar spreadsheet-like surface, while kanban, calendar, timeline, and dashboard views serve different roles.

Templates and automations can turn that surface into a capable system. A status change can notify a reviewer, assign the next owner, or update a date. This is especially useful when an agency's workflow is unusual and the team is willing to maintain its own operating model.

sections.heading: What specialist context changes
paragraphs: A board item can represent a video, but it does not inherently understand the customer conversation that created it or the payout that follows approved delivery. Agencies compensate by adding columns, connected boards, integrations, and conventions. Each addition can work, but together they require governance.

Gigxomi starts with the editing business as the data model. Customer lanes, managers, editors, production work, review, delivery, accounting, and payouts belong to the same operating story. For agencies with a standard service model, this can be more valuable than unlimited board flexibility.

sections.heading: Calculate workflow maintenance honestly
paragraphs: List every board, mirror column, automation, integration, and dashboard the editing operation needs. Estimate who tests changes and resolves broken recipes. Then compare that ongoing responsibility with the specialist product's fit gaps. A general platform is economical when the custom model produces real advantage; it is expensive when it merely reconstructs common agency behavior.

Also examine reporting quality. A beautiful dashboard built on inconsistently updated columns creates confidence without truth. During a trial, sample ten projects and compare displayed state with the latest customer decision, editor ownership, and delivered file. Accuracy matters more than presentation.

sections.heading: Migration plan from monday.com
paragraphs: Export active production boards with stable identifiers, but do not assume every column deserves a destination. Classify fields as essential operating data, useful historical context, obsolete workaround, or calculated reporting. Move the first category, archive the second, delete the third only after review, and rebuild the fourth from trustworthy source data.

Choose one board owner and one Gigxomi owner for cutover. Route all new editing enquiries into the selected source of truth, then close active monday.com items as each project completes. Preserve company-wide boards if other departments rely on them, and publish only milestone summaries back to leadership reporting.

sections.heading: Best fit by agency maturity
paragraphs: monday.com fits agencies that have an operations function, want visual configurability, and coordinate different services through shared dashboards. It can also fit a unique production methodology that would feel constrained by specialist defaults.

Gigxomi fits agencies whose complexity comes less from unusual process design and more from fragmented systems. If owners repeatedly connect social messages, project boards, editors, review status, and payout spreadsheets by hand, a domain operating system deserves a serious pilot.

Who maintains automations and connected-board logic?

How are editor payouts linked to approved work?
Which monday.com boards must remain for non-production teams?
